o: We repeatedly delete the closest removable duplicate: scanning left to right, at the first character that has an equal character within distance k (in the current string), delete that later duplicate. Example 3 shows deletions cascade: removing the second 'y' brings a third 'y' within range of the first, so it gets deleted too. Brute-force simulation rescans the string after each deletion (O(n) deletions × O(n) scan). The efficient view: track, for each letter, the position of its currently kept occurrence; a new occurrence is deleted iff its current rank distance to that kept occurrence is ≤ k. A Fenwick tree over original positions gives current ranks in O(log n), since deletions only shift characters to the left of a position.
k: Only the most recent kept occurrence of each letter matters: any closer older duplicate would already have been merged into it.
Current-string distance between two surviving positions equals the difference of their alive-ranks, computable with a Fenwick tree.
Deletions never move characters rightward, so processing positions left to right with live rank queries simulates the exact operation order.

a.i: Keep the string as a mutable list. Repeatedly scan for the smallest index i whose nearest equal neighbor within k exists, delete that neighbor, and restart. This literally implements the specified procedure and is easy to reason about.
s: Scan i from left; for each i check positions i+1..i+k for an equal character.
On the first hit, delete that position and restart the scan.
When a full scan finds nothing, join and return.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — up to n deletions, each triggering an O(n) rescan (string erase is O(n)). Acceptable given typical test data, risky at the limit.

a.i: Process original positions left to right. Maintain a BIT holding 1 for each alive position, and prev[c] = position of the kept occurrence of letter c. At position i with letter c, its current rank is qry(i); the kept occurrence's current rank is qry(prev[c]). If the rank gap is ≤ k, delete i (BIT update −1); otherwise keep it and set prev[c] = i. This reproduces the mandated operation order exactly, because deletions to the left are precisely what shrink current distances.
s: Initialize a BIT of all ones and an empty prev map.
For each position i in order: compute r_i = qry(i).
If c ∈ prev and r_i − qry(prev[c]) ≤ k, mark i dead and update the BIT by −1.
Otherwise set prev[c] = i; finally output all alive characters.
a.t: O(n log n) — one BIT query/update pair per character.

w: Note the C++ listing above keeps a small redundant loop; the core logic (prev array + BIT ranks, appending kept characters) is complete and correct. In an interview, present the simulation first to establish the operation semantics, then optimize with the rank-tracking insight. Pitfalls: using original index differences instead of current-string distances (wrong after deletions), and updating prev[c] on a deleted character (the kept occurrence must remain the anchor). Edge cases: k ≥ n collapses every repeated letter to one occurrence; strings with all distinct letters return unchanged. Follow-up: what if merges could chain across different letters, or k changes between operations?
